overview.description: Camicia (Italian for 'Shirt') is a simple game of pure luck for two players. It is the Italian version of Beggar My Neighbour. Players turn over cards alternately; Aces, 2s and 3s are 'attack' cards that force the opponent to play 1, 2, or 3 cards respectively. If the defender cannot play an attack card in response, the attacker wins the pile.

history.origins: Camicia is the Italian version of Beggar My Neighbour (also known as Strip Jack Naked or Beat Your Neighbor Out of Doors), a traditional children's card game played worldwide. The name 'Camicia' means 'shirt' in Italian, possibly referring to the idea of stripping your opponent of cards.
timeline: Traditional origins: Played for generations in Italy
Modern: Known as Italian variant of Beggar My Neighbour
Current: Still played as children's game in Italy
history.evolution: The game follows the same basic structure as Beggar My Neighbour, using the Italian 40-card deck instead of the standard 52-card deck. The attack cards (A, 2, 3) and their values are consistent with the international version.
history.cultural: Camicia is primarily a children's game in Italy, played for fun with no skill involved. It serves as an introduction to card games for young children due to its simple rules.

setup.players: Camicia is played by exactly two players. Each player receives an equal share of the deck face down (20 cards each with a 40-card Italian deck, or 26 each with 52 cards). Players keep their cards in a packet and do not look at them; they take turns turning the top card face up onto the table.
setup.deck: 40-card Italian deck (suits: swords, batons, cups, coins) or 52-card standard deck. Suits are ignored. Attack cards: Aces, 2s, 3s. Normal cards: 4-10, J, Q, K (or 4-7, J, Q, K in 40-card deck).
setup.dealing: All cards dealt face down to the two players, 20 cards each (if 40-card deck) or 26 cards each (if 52-card deck). Players do not look at their cards.

rules.objective: Win all the cards. The player who runs out of cards loses.
rules.gameplay: Players alternate turning the top card of their packet face up onto a central pile. Normal cards (non-attack): no action, play passes to opponent. Attack cards (A, 2, 3): opponent must play 1, 2, or 3 cards respectively. If all response cards are normal, attacker takes the entire pile and places it face down under their packet. If opponent plays an attack card during response, the original attack is cancelled and the new attack takes effect (the previous attacker must now respond). Continue until one player runs out of cards.
keyRules: Attack cards: Aces (1 card), 2s (2 cards), 3s (3 cards)
Turn cards face up to central pile alternately
Attack forces opponent to play 1-3 cards
If defender plays attack card, new attack supersedes old
If defender plays all normal cards, attacker wins pile
Won cards go face down under winner's packet
First player out of cards loses

strategy.basic: There is no strategy in Camicia - it is a game of pure luck. The outcome is determined entirely by the order of cards in the initial deal.
strategy.intermediate: While no decisions are made during play, understanding the probabilities can be interesting. Attack cards (A, 2, 3) become diluted as you win cards, making you more vulnerable. Threes are most valuable but also most vulnerable to counterattack.
strategy.advanced: No advanced strategy exists as players make no choices. The game is mathematically deterministic based on initial card distribution.
tips: Game is pure luck - no decisions to make
Attack cards become diluted as you win piles
Threes are powerful but vulnerable to counterattack
Aces are safest but capture fewest cards
Game can last a long time due to card recycling
Good game for young children learning cards

engine.deckDescription: A stripped French deck containing 40 cards with four suits (Hearts, Diamonds, Clubs, Spades) and eight ranks per suit (6 through Ace), created by removing all 2s through 5s from a standard 52-card deck.
engine.suitDescription: Four traditional French suits: Hearts (Cœur), Diamonds (Carreau), Clubs (Trèfle), and Spades (Pique), each represented with standard French card iconography and distinct color coding for easy recognition during gameplay.
engine.rankDescription: Eight ranks per suit in ascending order: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, Jack (Valet), Queen (Dame), King (Roi), and Ace as the highest card, where each rank determines card strength and eligibility for building sequences.
